title: Which jobs run when one fails

blocks.text: Before the trim planner's workflow goes live, the team wants to answer "if this job fails, what still runs?" for any workflow, without pushing commits to find out. Model GitHub's rule from the lesson.

In `job_outcomes.py`, write `outcomes(jobs, event, failing=frozenset())`. `jobs` maps each job's name to its settings: `needs` (one name or a list, maybe missing) and `if` (maybe missing). It returns each job's outcome for one event: `"success"`, `"failure"` or `"skipped"`. A job that runs ends in `"failure"` if its name is in `failing`, and in `"success"` otherwise.

items: An `if` of the form `github.event_name == 'NAME'` skips the job when the event is not `NAME`.
A job whose needs did not all succeed (one failed, or one was skipped) is skipped, unless its `if` contains `always()`, which runs it whatever its needs did.

An `if` may hold both, joined by `&&` (`always() && github.event_name == 'push'`). Both parts must hold: the event test is applied first, so on another event the job is skipped even with `always()`; on the named event, `always()` runs it whatever its needs did.
The dict may list a job before the jobs it needs; decide each job only after its needs.

blocks.text: You may assume the needs form no cycle and name only jobs in `jobs`. `EVENT` and `needs_of` are given; about 15 lines remain.

cases.says: a push runs all three jobs; a pull request skips image and deploy
a failed test skips build, and the deploy that needs only build
a job whose need was skipped is skipped, not run
a job with always() runs after its need failed
the outcome does not depend on the order the jobs are listed in
one failed need among several skips the job
an if that holds both always() and an event test still skips the job on another event
